chunks: Choosing a board stackup. The question: How to choose board stackup?
Choosing a stackup means deciding the order of the board's layers and how thick the insulation between them is.
A good order puts a solid copper plane (usually ground) right next to every signal layer, so each fast signal has a short, well-defined path home.
It also keeps the stack symmetric and uses thicknesses the fab can build at a sensible cost.
Hold your hand just above a table under a ceiling lamp. Its shadow is small and sharp, right under your hand.
Lift your hand high and the shadow spreads out and overlaps the shadows of things nearby.
A signal's return current behaves the same way: it flows in the plane under the trace, tight when the plane is close and spread wide when it is far.
The analogy breaks in one place: the return current is a real current, so the plane under it must be unbroken.
Return current hugs the trace: 50% within ±1h, 79. 5% within ±3h, 94% within ±10h. A trace 0. 2 mm above a plane has most of its return within about 0. 6 mm either side.
The same trace 1. 6 mm above a plane spreads its return over ±5 mm, so adjacent traces share return current and cross-talk.
Reference plane: the solid ground or power layer next to a signal layer, where its return current flows ("Which layers should be ground").
Return current: the current flowing back to the source, completing the circuit. Crosstalk: a signal leaking into a neighboring trace.
Plane pair: a power plane right next to a ground plane, which acts as a small built-in capacitor ("Which layers for power planes").
Symmetric stackup: the same layer thicknesses mirrored around the center, so the board stays flat.
The page uses a rule for how far the return current spreads: about 80% of it flows within three times the trace's height on either side. For a trace 0.
2 mm above its plane, that is within 0. 6 mm either side. For a trace 1. 6 mm above its plane, it spreads over 4.
8 mm either side, so neighbors share return current and crosstalk grows.
That is why a 4-layer board uses signal, ground, power, signal, with thin insulation between each outer layer and its plane. That is the whole idea.

"I'd start with a few rules: every signal layer next to a solid reference plane, power and ground planes adjacent and tightly coupled, a symmetric stack so the board stays flat, and dielectric thicknesses that give sensible trace widths for 50 ohms.
For four layers that's signal, ground, power, signal. For six, signal, ground, signal, power, ground, signal.
Then I get the fab's real thicknesses and permittivity and run the impedance calculation on those."
